## Session 30b: a plan's derivation over values, upstream

24 November 2026 · branch `claude/s30b-visits-upstream-eca89b` · [#180](https://github.com/joshbotts/FRUS-Explorer-Web-App/pull/180) · upstream `0b839bde` since S26b's #171, unchanged here; [FRUS-Explorer#1988](https://github.com/joshbotts/FRUS-Explorer/pull/1988), merged

**Since merged** (S27c's pin move records it): the owner merged FRUS-Explorer#1988 on 24 November (23:01 UTC) as `efd73ecb`, the batch's last, whose tree is its head's, `b73454d4`, onto `v2` at `807d0c05`, the branch's base, so Mac check 41 is done and the Next below with it. S27c's pin move took it, to `efd73ecb`, `v2`'s head, with nothing of the web's to change for it, as above.

Phase 4's row S30b, the second upstream batch's last, cut once S30a's #1981 had merged: an Archives Visit plan's derivation runs in FRUSCoreKit over the research export's records of a plan, its documents and its targets, and the plan's writes are rules there that answer the rows to write, so that the Visits track (S30c, S30d) derives a plan and writes its rows, ids and all, as the app does. The pull request is `claude/archive-visit-derivation-kit`, cut from `v2` at `3b2d299f` (S28a's #1985) and moved, before it opened, onto `807d0c05` (S29b's #1987, which merged during the session and changed none of its code files). It is labelled `Mac`, its body asks for Mac verification and lists Mac check 41, and it is not merged. Under rule 4 it changes shared files, and this repository changes only its records.

**What moved:**
- **FRUSCoreKit (`TripPacket/`), by `git mv`, public:** `ArchiveVisitDerivation`, with `ArchiveVisitTargetKeys` and `ArchiveVisitTopicReseed`. `derive`, its overlay (`overlay(for:over:)`, which a host can read again after a write of stored state alone), the join of the stored rows to the derived keys (`ArchiveVisitTargetKeys.resolve` and `shownRow`) and the input's signature read `ArchiveVisitPlanExport` with its `ArchiveVisitDocumentExport` seeds and `ArchiveVisitTargetExport` stored targets, which carry every field they read. `derive` takes the bundled indexes the builder reads (`TripPacketIndexes`) and is `@MainActor`, as the builder and its data source are; the rest is nonisolated. The signature is counted by one rule over values (`inputSignature(seeds:inquiryText:tiers:targets:indexedVolumeIds:)`), which the records' form and the app's form over its rows both call, the app's still reading three attributes of each seed row and six of each state row on every pass of a view's body.

## Session 26c: the vectors on the server

24 November 2026 · branch `claude/s26c-vectors-server-8a8ec6` · [#177](https://github.com/joshbotts/FRUS-Explorer-Web-App/pull/177) · upstream `0b839bde`, unchanged

Phase 4's row S26c, in wave 4 beside S29d on the language track and S29b upstream: the semantic vectors on the server, every one in the image, by the owner's answers of 23 November. No upstream pull request, no pin move and no migration. The branch was cut from `main` at `19f0520`, #175's merge, which `main` still was at the push.

**The bundled tier, read once for both** (`Sources/FRUSLightCore/SemanticVectors.swift`, `Sources/FRUSLightAPI/SemanticMap.swift`):
- **`SemanticVectors`,** an actor, one a server (`ServerComponents.vectors`), reads the bundled pair on its first use, off the cooperative pool, through the kit's `SemanticBundledTiers(indexAt:binaryAt:)`, S26a's: `semantic-vectors-index.json` decoded and `semantic-vectors-binary.bin` mapped, and refused as the kit refuses a pair whose digests differ. With it, the bundled `semantic-shards-manifest.json`, held to the pair's generation as the app holds it at wiring time; a manifest missing, undecodable or of another generation refuses the vectors, and a refused generation serves no shard.
- **The map reads its vectors' index from the same read.** S28b's `SemanticMapFiles` decoded the vectors' index itself; it now takes `tiers()`, so the pair is read once for the map and the vectors alike, and, as the app's map waits on `BundledSemanticVectors`, a pair the kit refuses draws no map: a missing vectors' file in the app's words for a missing map, anything else in its words for a map it cannot read, with the vectors' refusal after them. Every refusal S28b's tests named gives the words it gave, and two cases join them, the vectors' binary missing and of other vectors than its index; the map's tests link the bundled binary into their folders.

**The shards, in the image's read-only folder** (`/usr/share/frus-light/semantic/shards`, `ServerConfiguration.semanticShards`, which has no variable):
- **`SemanticVectors` answers SemanticVectorsKit's `SemanticShardSource`,** the one read FRUSCoreKit's semantic passes make of a host's shards (S26a), for S26d and S27d. The first time a volume's shard is asked for, it is opened through the kit's `SemanticShard`, which checks its magic, version, provenance digest, width, the bundled index's count and its length, and then held to the bundled manifest's length and SHA-256, as the app's fetcher holds a shard before its store keeps it; then it stays mapped, as the app's store keeps its shards. Concurrent first requests share one check. One refused is kept with why: not published, which is no fault; missing from the folder; refused by the kit; or not the manifest's bytes. The kit's checks come first, so that a shard of another generation is called one, not a shard that did not arrive intact.
- **The report checks every shard.** Before Vectors or `frus-light semantic` first answers, the server checks every published shard once, 162 MB hashed in about a second, keeping its verdict and not its mapping, so that what it says is the whole folder's, where the app's screen can say only what it has noticed. The status reads the folder's listing and hashes nothing.

**The image** (`docker/Dockerfile`, `docker/fetch-vectors`, `NOTICE`):
- **The vectors' host, recorded beside the pin:** `ARG VECTORS_REPOSITORY=joshbotts/frus-semantic-vectors`, `VECTORS_COMMIT=9be645e9c0d6c5beb6aef998416fd3304de52761`, the commit whose `generations/89481b18/shards-manifest.json` is the pinned bundled manifest byte for byte (SHA-256 `a8ed3e80…`, read again on 24 November), and `VECTORS_BASE_COMMIT`, the generation's first publication, the same commit at the pin, the folder's only one. `VectorsImageTests` holds the repository and the generation to the app's `SemanticShardFetcher.defaultBaseURL` and the bundled index's provenance, and COORDINATION §5's pin-move checklist gains the line that records the host's commit when the bundled `semantic-*` files move.
- **The vectors stage** runs `docker/fetch-vectors`, one script for the image's stage and for CI: it fetches the two commits' manifests and refuses `VECTORS_COMMIT`'s unless it is the bundled one byte for byte; fetches the base's every shard and, at `VECTORS_COMMIT`, those its manifest names with another length or digest, or adds, from `raw.githubusercontent.com` at each commit, eight at a time; holds each to its manifest's length and SHA-256; and lays them out in two folders, each file mode 0444 and each folder 0755, each with the day its manifest names, so that a build whose shards and bundled files disagree fails. Given a folder as its `vectors-source` context, as CI gives the Actions cache's copy, it fetches only what the folder lacks or holds damaged. `docker/fetch-vectors selftest` runs it over a host of its own, a re-pack among it: the base layer the first publication, the re-pack's the changed and added shards, a second run the same bytes, modes and times and fetching nothing, a damaged cache file fetched again, and another manifest and a damaged shard refused.
- **Two layers,** `COPY --link --from=vectors /out/base/ /` and `/out/repack/ /`, after the model's: the generation's 553 shards as first published, 164 MB unpacked and 121.7 MB to pull (`sha256:1f936b4b97636cd5…`), and those a re-pack has changed or added since, none at the pin, its folders alone, 24.6 kB unpacked and 174 bytes to pull (`sha256:6c9801414cfc8ebd…`). Measured: the image built from the folder `docker/fetch-vectors` had filled, as CI builds it, and built again with the vectors stage rebuilt from nothing and no folder, fetching the 553 from the host (in 19 s), had the same digest in each of its eleven layers, the two shards' layers among them. The stage runs on the build platform and `COPY --link` makes its layers apart from those below them, so both architectures' images carry the same two, which `image.yml` builds on `main`.
- **Its size, on arm64:** 816 MB unpacked and 535 MB to pull (534,509,679 bytes of layers), where S27b's image was 648 MB and 410 MB: the shards' base layer 164 MB unpacked and 122 MB to pull, and the rest S28b's, S29c's and this row's server. The model's layer is S27b's, `sha256:33271e45…`, unchanged, so that an install holding it pulls the shards' layers and the layers above them alone. Docker Desktop's "disk usage", 1.35 GB, adds the two.
- **`NOTICE`** names the shards, their folder and the host, whose own NOTICE says they are model outputs derived from the public-domain series, to which no model-licence conditions attach.

**CI** (`.github/workflows/ci.yml`, `image.yml`): the compose job and `image.yml`'s builds take the shards from the Actions cache by the bundled manifest's SHA-256, `semantic-vectors-<sha256>`, which `docker/fetch-vectors` fills once a manifest, and give them to the build as its `vectors-source` context, so that no CI build fetches a shard; the compose job runs the script's self-test first. The branch was cut from `main` at `42c178e`, which holds S27b's #166, whose line in `Package.swift` gives `FRUSLightCore` and `FRUSLightAPI` SemanticVectorsKit; the kit's reader of the map, `SemanticMapVectors`, was public at the pin.

**The library: WebGL2 alone, not deck.gl.** Before anything was built on deck.gl, a probe drew the bundled map's 314,616 points two ways from the same bytes: with deck.gl 9.4.1, its `ScatterplotLayer` under an `OrthographicView` (`@deck.gl/core` and `@deck.gl/layers`, which bring luma.gl 9.4.2 and loaders.gl 4.5.4, 33 packages, each resolved to a version published before 9 November); and with WebGL2 alone, as the app's Metal renderer draws. Each page was served under the app's policy word for word (`WebClient.policy`) and opened in Playwright's Chromium, as the browser suite opens the app, with every console message and every `securitypolicyviolation` event kept. deck.gl draws under the policy: no violation and no console error. Its bundle carries loaders.gl's worker made from a blob and luma.gl's Spector hook, which a scatter of typed arrays never reaches. It was not used, for what it costs. A frame below is drawn and then read back by one pixel, which waits for the GPU to finish it, since Chromium's `finish()` returns at once:

| The 314,616 points | WebGL2 alone | deck.gl 9.4.1 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A frame on the owner's Mac: Google Chrome 157, headless, ANGLE on Metal, the M5; 1920 × 1280 pixels | median 1.2 ms, p95 2.9 | median 5.4 ms, p95 11.3 |
| A frame under the browser suite's renderer: Playwright 1.63's Chromium 153 in its image, SwiftShader on ANGLE's Vulkan, on this Mac's arm64; 960 × 640 | median 35.5 ms, p95 43.2 | median 4.9 s, p95 5.5 s, the fastest 2.0 s |
| The page's heap once drawn, on the Mac | 2.1 MB more | 17.3 MB more |
| Script | about 3 KB | 594 KB, 167 KB gzipped, and a 97 KB chunk beside it |

Under the software renderer, which CI's browser suite draws with, as does any browser without a usable GPU, the first probe's 160 frames of deck.gl did not finish in 280 seconds. Its scatter draws an instanced quad a point through a projection written for maps; the app's renderer draws one point sprite a point in one draw call, and WebGL2 does the same, from the server's six bytes a point as they arrive. So `web/package.json` is unchanged, and phase 4 adds no browser library, where PLAN's rule 3 for phase 4 had this row add deck.gl. The probe's pages, its results and its screenshots are in the shared notes folder, `s28b-probe/`.

**The server** (`Sources/FRUSLightAPI/SemanticMap.swift`, and a line in `Routes.swift` beside the analytics'):
- **`GET /api/v1/semantic/map`**: the 314,616 points as one binary answer, `application/octet-stream`, six bytes a point in the bundled vectors' row order, little-endian: `int16` x and y on the map's grid and the `uint16` region, `0xFFFF` between regions. It is the placement block of `semantic-map.bin` as the kit's `SemanticMapVectors` reads it, 1,887,696 bytes.
- **`GET /api/v1/semantic/map/regions`**: the 140 regions of `semantic-map-index.json`, by id, each with its four terms, its count, its centre and its eras' counts, and the layout's facts: its identity, the day it was made, the documents, the 88,059 between regions, the grid's extent of 30,000, and how it was made and clustered.
- **Read once and refused whole.** `SemanticMapFiles`, an actor, reads the three files on the first request, off the cooperative pool, and keeps the answers. It refuses the map as the app's `BundledSemanticMap.prepare()` does, both answers alike, 503 `SEMANTIC_MAP_UNAVAILABLE`: when the map's index or its binary names other vectors than the bundled vectors' index's provenance, when the binary places another number of documents than the vectors hold, or when a file is missing or unreadable. It also refuses an index whose count, grid or number of regions is not the binary's. The refusals are in the app's words (`SemanticMapSpikeView.describe`), "This build" a server, with the file and the reason after them.
- **Revalidated, not resent.** Each answer carries an entity tag of its own bytes (FNV-1a, as the reader tags its pages), with `Cache-Control: private, no-cache`, and answers 304 to a request that holds it. So a browser keeps an answer until the layout changes or a later row changes the answer's form. The regions are encoded once, their keys sorted, so that their bytes, and their tag, are the same at every start.

**The browser app** (`web/src/analytics/SemanticAnalyticsScreen.tsx`, `SemanticMap.tsx`, `semanticMapRenderer.ts`, `semanticMapRules.ts`, `web/src/api/semanticMap.ts`; lines in `router.tsx`, `shell/AppShell.tsx`, `copy.ts` and `styles/app.css`):
- **Semantic Analytics, `/analytics/semantic`.** The header's Analytics menu lists it fifth, after Archival Analytics and before the divider, as the Mac's menu does.
- **The renderer: WebGL2 alone, as the app's Metal renderer draws.** The server's answer is the vertex buffer as it came: x and y read as floats, the region as an integer. The shader gives each point the Regions lens's slot, 0 between regions and otherwise one of the other fifteen in turn. Each point is a round sprite of two of the canvas's own pixels with the app's soft edge. It is drawn in the app's sixteen-slot palette on the app's dark ground (0.06, 0.07, 0.09) in either appearance, with the app's blending, in one draw call, and only when the view changes. The drawing buffer is kept at the frame's size in the screen's pixels (`device-pixel-content-box`), its aspect kept where the GPU's limit is smaller. A new size, which clears the canvas, is drawn at once, before the browser paints, and nothing is drawn before the first size. A lost context is made again.
- **Pan and zoom.** The Mac's Zoom In and Zoom Out (its step of 1.4) and Fit the Map. With the map focused, the arrow keys move the view an eighth of its width or height, + and − zoom, and 0 or Home fits the map. A drag moves the map; the wheel, a pinch and a double click (the Mac's 1.6) zoom about the pointer. The zoom is said in a status line once it settles, the whole map or how many times in or out. The canvas is hidden from screen readers, as the app's is. The map is one stop, `role="application"`, named Semantic map and described by its keys.
- **The regions' table beside it**, largest first, ties by id, with the app's columns Region, Terms and Documents, under the summary the app's list of the regions opens with ("Semantic map: 140 regions covering 226,557 documents. 88,059 more sit between regions and are not listed. Position shows similarity, not time …"). The legend has the Regions lens's one entry, Between regions. Its caption is the app's, naming the table where the app's names the map, until S28c draws the names.
- **Without WebGL2:** the table and a sentence, and no points fetched. A WebGL2 that fails as the map is made gives the table and a sentence of its own, with the reason in the console.
- **Mirrored, until S28a moves the map's rules into the kit:** the palette, its `hsb` and a region's slot (`SemanticMapColouring`); the ground, the sprite, the projection, the blending and the one draw call (`SemanticMapRenderer`); the camera's scale (`SemanticMapCamera`), its fit and its pan; and the zoom steps (`SemanticMapSpikeView`). `SemanticMapMirrorParityTests` holds each pair to the app's lines, with the table's order and columns and every word copy.ts and the server take.

**Tests:**
- **`SemanticMapRouteTests` (3).** Over the bundled file, every one of the 314,616 points' place and region through the API equals the kit's `placement(at:)`, row for row. The regions are the index's and count the points, region by region, and those between. Each answer revalidates by a tag of its own bytes, the same when the map is read again, the regions' keys sorted; a HEAD says the answer's length; and a parameter is refused. The map is refused, both answers alike and in the app's words, for an index or a binary naming other vectors, vectors of another count, a binary cut short, an index of another grid, an index that is not one, and a missing binary or vectors' index.
- **`SemanticMapMirrorParityTests` (5)**, the mirror pairs above.
- **`semanticMapRules.test.ts` (11)**: the palette, its sweep and its slots; the swatch's colour; the camera's scale, its projection both ways, the zoom about a point that stays put, the limits, the pan by drag and by key; the zoom's words and the wheel.
- **`SemanticAnalytics.test.tsx` (4)**: the table, its order and its summary without WebGL2 and with no points fetched; a refusal; an answer of the wrong length; and a context that fails.
- **Playwright's `semantic-map.spec.ts`.** It opens the map from the Analytics menu by keyboard. It finds it drawn: more than a twentieth and less than nine-tenths of its frame the points' colours, a fifth when measured. It zooms and pans by keyboard: each frame differs from the last, and 0 draws the first frame again pixel for pixel. It uses the buttons, a drag and the wheel. It reads the table, 140 rows largest first, and checks axe. It prints what a frame costs, and fails if a key's frame takes a median of more than 1 s, ten times the budget below.

**Measured,** the shipped renderer (`semanticMapRenderer.ts`, through the probe), the points from the bundled file:
- **On the owner's Mac** (Google Chrome 157, headless, ANGLE on Metal, the M5; 960 × 640 at a device scale of 2, 1,920 × 1,280 pixels): a frame of 60 views in a median 0.8 ms (p95 2.6, the slowest 6.5), and of the whole map 0.7 ms (p95 1.6). It holds 60 frames a second, a median 16.7 ms apart. The page's script drew its first frame in 307 ms, 39 of them loading the map. The heap grew by 2.1 MB, the map's answer; the GPU holds the vertex buffer, 1.9 MB.
- **Under the browser suite's renderer** (Playwright 1.63's Chromium 153, SwiftShader, arm64; 960 × 640): a frame of 60 views in a median 24.8 ms (p95 58.0, the slowest 96.2), and of the whole map 36.7 ms (p95 60.3). Frames come a median 32 ms apart, about 31 a second. Chromium's GPU process grew from 66 to 175 MB and the page's process from 79 to 129 MB, the software renderer's buffers and compiled shaders among them, and the heap by 7.0 MB. Against the image, in the browser suite: the first frame 129 ms after the menu's Enter (141 under the path), and a key's frame done in a median 34.3 ms (34.6), the slowest 107.2 ms, 20.0% of the frame drawn.

**The budget the map keeps.** The points cost their answer once in the page and once in the GPU's buffer, 1.9 MB each, with nothing made per point. A frame is one draw call, drawn only when the view changes. On a GPU it fits a frame at 60 Hz many times over: the app measured 3.28 ms on an M1 Max's Metal, and the web 0.8 ms on the M5. Under a software renderer it stays within 100 ms, so that the map pans in any browser with WebGL2; the browser suite fails at ten times that.

**The review.** A cold review by a fresh agent, given the commit and not the session's reading of it, found no defect in what the code did, and three risks, each fixed before the push:
- **Tags.** Each tag came from the layout's identity alone, which a later change to an answer's form would have left stale in a browser, and the regions were encoded in an order of their eras' keys that moves at each start. Now each answer's tag is its bytes', and the regions are encoded once, their keys sorted.
- **Resizes.** A resize cleared the canvas a frame before it was drawn again, and a first frame could be drawn at the canvas's 300 × 150. Now a new size is drawn at once, and nothing is drawn before the first.
- **Drags.** A drag was left held when a context menu or the system took the mouse's release. Now a mouse with no button down ends it, so does a lost capture, and a Control-click moves nothing.

Its five nits were taken too: the shaders are deleted once linked; the buffer keeps its aspect under the GPU's limit; a WebGL2 that fails has a sentence of its own; the spec bounds the drawn share above and compares every move's frame; and a sideways scroll goes on to the page.

**The runs,** on the owner's Mac under the heavy lock, which S30a's Mac runs shared, from this entry's code:
- **Swift:** `scripts/swift test`, 4,440 tests, all passing; the skips are the PostgreSQL store's, without `--postgres`, and the one named skip.
- **The browser app:** typecheck, lint, the unit tests in 83 files, and the build.
- **The image and the smoke test:** `frus-light:s28b` in 2.5 minutes on the warm cache, then `FRUS_IMAGE=frus-light:s28b FRUS_HOST_PORT=18280 scripts/compose-smoke --e2e`. Its first run stopped where the Standalone project's mirror binds the next port, 18281, which the probe's own server held. Its second failed this row's spec where 0 should draw the first frame again: the focus ring follows the frame's rounded corners into the canvas's box, so the spec now compares frames with the map focused. Its third passed, in 9 minutes: the browser suite's 97 tests at the root and 97 under the path, this row's spec among them.
- **After the review's fixes,** in one hold (`.build/linux/s28b/review.sh`):
  - the browser app's steps, and the Swift build with the row's two suites passing;
  - the probe again, a frame of the whole map in a median 36.2 ms under SwiftShader;
  - the image, in a minute;
  - the smoke test, passing again with 97 and 97, a key's frame done in a median 52.6 ms at the root and 50.3 under the path.

**Records:** this entry and S28b's paragraph in `docs/PLAN.md`; and SPEC's line for the map, whose deck.gl is WebGL2 alone. SPEC's lines for the two routes, and the README's, are the S28 group's last row's, S28e's.

**Next:** on the Map track, S28c, after S27c's pin move: the map's reading, the lenses, the names and the cards, over this row's routes and renderer. A lens's slot computed on the server rides as a second vertex buffer, where the shader now takes the region's slot. The scope's ghost rides as a third, with the app's shader's rule. ## Session 29a: WordCloudKit takes its tagger from its host, upstream

23 November 2026 · branch `claude/s29a-tagger-seam-a350c3` · [#167](https://github.com/joshbotts/FRUS-Explorer-Web-App/pull/167) · upstream `4556c4d5`, unchanged; [FRUS-Explorer#1979](https://github.com/joshbotts/FRUS-Explorer/pull/1979), merged

**Since merged** (S26b's pin move records it): the owner merged FRUS-Explorer#1979 on the evening of 23 November (01:43 UTC on the 24th) as `070f2fcb`, the batch's first, whose tree is its head's, `b926e18b`, onto `v2` at `4556c4d5`, the branch's base, so Mac check 36 is done. S26b's pin move took it, to `0b839bde`, with `Package.swift` and the server's Word Cloud patched as below, the configuration given the file's tokenizer too (the log's entry, Session 26b).

Phase 4's row S29a, in wave 1 beside S26a and S27b: one upstream pull request in which WordCloudKit's tokenizers take their tagger from their host, so that the web's own tagger (S29c) counts through the kit's rules and the app's generator (S29d). It is `claude/wordcloudkit-host-tagger`, cut from `v2` at `4556c4d5`, which `v2` still is, in three commits: the change, the cold review's fixes, and the plan of record's entry; labelled `Mac`, its body asks for Mac verification and lists Mac check 36, and it is not merged. Under rule 4 it changes shared files, and this repository changes only its records.

**The seam:** `WordCloudTagger`, a protocol for what the two tokenizers read of `NLTagger`: each word of a text in order with its range and, when the walk asks (`WordCloudTagReading`), its lemma and its lexical class (`WordCloudLexicalClass`: noun, verb, adjective, other), and for the entity lenses each name, joined, with its type (`WordCloudNameType`). A tagger comes with its `NaturalLanguageHealth` and its `WordCloudTokenizerIdentity`, a name and a version. `NLTagger` conforms, walking itself with the calls the tokenizers made of it, its health the gate's verdict for the schemes it holds; `NaturalLanguageWordCloudTagger` asks the gate for a tagger for each walk with the schemes the walk reads. Both tokenizers count with any tagger, on every platform (`accumulate(from:into:tagger:)`, and the one pass's `accumulate(from:into:printedInto:tagger:)`); without one they count with NaturalLanguage's, as the app always has, and on Linux that form is unavailable and says why. A count of printed forms reads no lemma, whatever a tagger gives.

**The identity in the files:** `CloudVectorsFile.Provenance.tokenizer` and `KeynessBaselineFile.Configuration.tokenizer`. A stamp that names none was counted by NaturalLanguage at version 1, `WordCloudTokenizerIdentity.legacyNaturalLanguage`, fixed apart from `naturalLanguage`, and a stamp of that tokenizer is written without the key: so the four bundled files stand byte for byte, which two of the app's suites hold (they re-encode a bundled reference and compare its bytes, and failed the first commit's full run, which wrote the key always), and the app's generator writes the bytes it wrote. `mismatches(against:includeDiplomatic:lexiconsDigest:stopwordsDigest:tokenizer:)` takes the scope's tokenizer with no default, and refuses another's (`Mismatch.tokenizer`): SPEC's rule, now code. The app's lookup passes NaturalLanguage's; the Word Cloud's and Collocates' lists name the case (`wordcloud.keyness.mismatch.tokenizer`, "the reference was counted by another tokenizer"), which the app's own counts never meet.

**The runner:** `CloudVectorsRunner.run(tagger:cloudLenses:environment:)` takes the tagger (its health refused on by the old rule, its identity stamped on every file), the lenses the clouds carry (the four by default, any of the six the run counts, each once) and the environment from its caller; `run()` passes NaturalLanguage's and the four. Every pass is bound to the run's tagger. For NaturalLanguage a run takes `NaturalLanguageWordCloudTagger`, not an `NLTagger`, whose schemes are fixed: the verification walks read no lemma scheme. The core builds on Linux (an `autoreleasepool` stand-in), and a run can be driven from a test at last.

**The suites:** `WordCloudTaggerTests.swift`, 33 tests in 4 suites, 25 of them wherever the kit builds over a stand-in tagger of tables, which is what WordCloudKit's suites gain on Linux; on Apple platforms, `NLTagger`'s word and name walks held to the calls the tokenizers made before. `CloudVectorsHostedRunTests.swift`, 11 tests: whole runs over a stand-in tagger in a folder of their own. `WordCloudMultiLensParityTests`, `WordCloudPrintedFormParityTests` and `CloudVectorsGeneratorTests` pass unchanged, the last's two scans of `run()`'s text among them; `WordCloudKitHostTests` passes the scope's tokenizer to `mismatches`. Twelve mutations, each failing a test.

**One cold review,** given the diff and none of this session's conclusions, found no change in the app's counts, compared call by call with `v2`, and seven points, six taken in the second commit: an `NLTagger`'s health was the process's verdict whatever its schemes; a file naming no tokenizer read as whatever `naturalLanguage` would become (now the fixed legacy identity); a tautological test (replaced by the walk-against-the-old-calls tests) and a verification test that could not fail (now a tagger whose printed walk differs is refused); a printed count trusted the tagger not to give lemmas; and docs. ## Session 29c: the web's tagger

24 November 2026 · branch `claude/s29c-web-tagger-4d39e8` · [#174](https://github.com/joshbotts/FRUS-Explorer-Web-App/pull/174) · upstream `0b839bde`, S26b's, unchanged

Phase 4's row S29c, in wave 2 beside S28b and S30a: the web's tagger, `Sources/FRUSLanguage`, the web's own as the rich-text codec is, since Linux has no NaturalLanguage and its Foundation splits no text into words. No upstream pull request, no pin move, no migration and no Dockerfile change. Cut from `main` at `42c178e`, pin `4556c4d5`, it merged `main` once when GitHub reported a conflict, after S26b's pin move to `0b839bde` had landed: three checkpoint rows of PLAN, each side's own kept.

**The owner's answers of 24 November,** asked once the three parts were built and tested, before anything was downloaded: MASC confirmed, having read its licence on the American National Corpus's own site, where https://anc.org/data/masc/ says anyone may download it for any purpose under the Creative Commons Attribution 3.0 United States licence, and https://www.anc.org/data/masc/about/ that it is distributed without licence or other restrictions; and WordNet 3.0's database from Princeton, under the licence https://wordnet.princeton.edu/license-and-commercial-use gives. The question also named what the ANC's own structure page says of MASC's general tags, that they "have not been fully hand-corrected", and so that the training would take the Penn Treebank project's tags of MASC's syntax, which its page links, where a text has them. Fetched that day and never committed: `MASC-3.0.0.tgz` (37,616,026 bytes, SHA-256 `206d8751…589d0c`) and `penn-treebank.tgz` (2,965,271 bytes, `65ae26e4…9f6230`) from the GitHub release the ANC's download page links, and `WordNet-3.0.tar.gz` (11,537,239 bytes, `640db279…3d3a52`) from wordnetcode.princeton.edu, whose download page sits behind a bot check the session did not pass; each archive's entries checked for unsafe paths and extracted under `.build/`, which git ignores.

**The splitter,** `WordSplitter`, over Unicode scalars, by six rules written down at the head of its file and held by `WordSplitterTests`. Probes of NaturalLanguage on this Mac (macOS 27.2.1) set them first: it splits clitics as the Penn Treebank does (`do` `n't`, `ca` `n't`, `Department` `’s`, `it` `'s`), keeps a hyphenated word whole only after `un`, `co`, `non` or `anti` in lowercase, keeps `1,500` and `3.5` whole and splits `10:30`, and keeps some abbreviations' periods and not others. The fixture volumes then settled the periods: of their 14,000 periods after a word, NaturalLanguage keeps one after a title (Mr. 1,392 times, Dr., Gen., Capt., Mrs., Col., Lt.), after the initials A B D E F G I K L M O Q S T U Z but not C H J N P R V W before a capital (`H.` of "H. A. Herbert" is `H` `.`), after an initialism but p.m., U.N. and U.S.S.R. before a capital or a number, and after any word when what follows is a lowercase word, a comma, a colon, a semicolon, a dash or a slash ("Libya. b."), never before a capital otherwise; it keeps `IL-28’s` whole, splits French's elided `d’` and `l’`, and makes a fraction a word of its own. Those are the rules. It splits 6.9 to 8.7 million words a second on one core.

**The tagger,** an averaged perceptron (Honnibal 2013's algorithm and features, with a word's shape added), whose weights are integers and whose sums are 64-bit, so a model scores the same on every architecture, and whose training shuffles by SplitMix64 from a seed, so a text and its settings make the same model byte for byte. It reads the typewriter's punctuation for the typographer's (`’s` as `'s`), which MASC mostly prints and FRUS does not. `frus-language train` re-splits each training text with the web's own splitter and gives each token the tag of the training token it overlaps most, so the model learns on the tokens it will tag: MASC 3.0.0's written genres, 376 texts, 328 with the Penn Treebank project's tags (its leaves found in each text with 1 in 50 missing at most; the treebank's own spellings such as `RSQUO` for `’` read) and 48 with MASC's own `-penn.xml` tags; 4,740 paragraphs, 479 left out for holding a word no training token covers (an email's headers, mostly); 371,655 tokens, 92.5% of them split as the text splits them; 52 tags; 5 passes, seed 1. Held out, every tenth paragraph: 0.931 of the tags right, 0.953 of NaturalLanguage's classes and 0.961 of the lenses' four. The model is 1,602,466 bytes, 105,155 features, 406,704 weights and a tag dictionary of 1,016 words, SHA-256 `fa42bd876c05…`, compiled in as `EmbeddedModel.swift` (2.1 MB of base64) with its provenance. Each tag has a class in NaturalLanguage's names (a possessive pronoun its determiner, `that` and the subordinators its prepositions, a list's marker its number), and three rules read more: `TO` is a particle before a verb's base form, `CD` holding a comma or a period another word, and a proper noun WordNet lists as an adjective, before a common noun in lowercase, an adjective ("Libyan government", where "Soviet Union" stays a noun).

**The lemmatizer,** WordNet 3.0's morphy as `morph.c` runs it for one word, over the exception lists and the single words of the four indexes (noun 2,011 exceptions and 57,506 lemmas, verb 2,321 and 8,700, adjective 1,489 and 20,983, adverb 7 and 3,767; 965,736 bytes, SHA-256 `56708897…`), compiled in as `EmbeddedWordNet.swift` with WordNet's licence, read by the tagger's class. Before morphy, NaturalLanguage's reading of FRUS as the fixtures measured it: a modal is its own lemma but `could` → `can`, `people` → `person`, and a word in capitals takes no detachment ("FMS" has none, where `s` would make "fm"); after it, an adjective in `ed` or `ing` WordNet does not list takes the verb's lemma, and a word holding `’` with no other lemma is itself with `'`, as NaturalLanguage gives "O'Neil", so that a word cloud keeps it. A name WordNet does not know has no lemma, as NaturalLanguage gives none: a rule that gave such a name itself made Bluefields and Cabezas disagree 567 times, and came out. The clitics have NaturalLanguage's lemmas (`n't` → `not`), and a word of a closed class is itself lowercased.

**The family:** `LanguageTagger.shared`, `FRUSLanguage 1+fa42bd87.56708897`, the version the rules' (`LanguageTagger.rulesVersion`, 1, raised with any change of rule) and the first eight hex digits of the model's and the lists' SHA-256. It lemmatizes and classifies words and names no one. `enumerateWords(in:reading:using:)` is S29a's `WordCloudTagger` walk, closure for closure, `LanguageReading` its option set bit for bit and `LexicalClass.lensClass` its four classes; the adapter of a dozen lines S29d writes after S26b's pin move is in the file's head.

**The Mac's tags:** `tools/mac-golden tags` indexes the three fixture volumes with the app's own pipeline and walks each document's body text as the pinned `WordCloudTokenizer` walks one for a part-of-speech lens, through the readiness gate, refusing a gate that would give no lemma. The session ran `scripts/make-golden`, the source half, on the owner's Mac (macOS 27.2.1, Xcode 27.2) under the heavy lock, in 4 min 53 s: 393 documents, 389,315 words, `fixtures/golden/language/tags.json`, 3,450,921 bytes, its words a line a document; every other golden file came out byte for byte, and check-golden passes. After the merge of `main` the session ran it again at `0b839bde`: every golden file but this one came out byte for byte S26b's, the tags changed in their provenance alone (the pin and the source digest), and the report was the same. It is a golden file made from the app's source, so a pin move's `scripts/make-golden` makes it again; FRUS body texts hold no line feed, so the tagger reads each document as one unit.

**The agreement,** `frus-parity language-report`, over the 393 documents, each body text held to the one the Mac tagged by its SHA-256 (information, as SPEC has it, not a check), which the owner accepted on 24 November:
- **Words (the splitter):** 389,114 split alike, 99.95% of the Mac's 389,315 and of the web's 389,322. What is left is mostly `No.` and `p.` before a number, which NaturalLanguage keeps or splits by context.
- **Lexical classes (the tagger):** 95.88% of the words split alike agree, 96.80% in the lenses' four: nouns 96.88% of the Mac's (95.32% of the web's), verbs 97.26% (96.49%), adjectives 84.90% (87.50%), others 98.38% (99.26%). By NaturalLanguage's class: determiners 99.11%, conjunctions 98.76%, pronouns 98.27%, prepositions 98.04%, verbs 97.26%, nouns 96.88%, particles 95.32%, numbers 91.99%, adverbs 86.02%, adjectives 84.90%, other words 47.88%, interjections 26.48%. The commonest differences are closed-class words (`that`, `all`, `to`, `as`, `such`), adverbs and adjectives (`more`, `most`), demonyms NaturalLanguage calls adjectives (Arab, Libyan before a capital) and `No` at a heading's start, its interjection.
- **Lemmas (the lemmatizer):** 94.30% the same lemma and 96.83% counted in the same form, the form a word cloud counts, the lemma or the word plural-folded: nouns 98.86% in the same form, verbs 98.48%, adjectives 97.64%, adverbs 97.92%; pronouns 72.43%, whose lemmas NaturalLanguage folds (`we` → `I`) and which no word cloud counts.
- **The rounds:** the first model gave 99.68%, 95.12%, 96.25%, 92.93% and 96.37%; the rules above, each taken from the report's commonest differences, gave the rest.
- **Speed:** 730,887 words tagged a second, and 764,730 in the run after the merge, split, tagged and lemmatized, on one core of the owner's M5 under Docker (arm64, release), the fixtures' 389,322 words in about half a second; splitting alone, 7 million.

**One cold review,** given the diff and the repository's rules and none of this session's conclusions, found the trainer keying its tag dictionary by each token as printed while the tagger reads a word by its typewriter's form, so that an entry for `’s` or `—` could never match: keyed as the tagger reads it, with `’s` and `'s` one entry, and the model trained again, the figures above being the retrained model's (its classes 95.93% before). It found too a word beginning with a hyphen read as hyphenated (`--`), the model's and the golden file's decoders trapping on an overflowing number where they should refuse it, an unguarded count of weights, and four nits, each fixed and tested; and it found nothing that would make the model or the digest differ between amd64 and arm64.

**The self-test:** `frus-light language-selftest`, registered beside `semantic`, reads no configuration and tags `LanguageSelftest.text`, a paragraph of every rule's cases, printing the family, the model's and the lists' digests and the SHA-256 of what it made, `ed5b99ff30f2cef2…3bfb`, which `fixtures/language/selftest.sha256` commits; `--expect` holds it there. `EmbeddedLanguageTests` holds the swift job to it, and the smoke test's new install step holds the hardened image's binary to it: on arm64 this Mac's hardened container printed it, and CI's compose job holds amd64's to it, as `image.yml`'s verify holds both on `main`. The model and the lists add about 3 MB to the server's binary, 103,587,496 bytes stripped on arm64.

**The tool,** `frus-language` (`Tests/FRUSLanguageTool`): `wordnet`, `train` (MASC's GrAF and treebank, CoNLL-U, or a word-tag list), `evaluate`, `tag` and `selftest`; and `frus-parity language-report [--model <file>]` scores a candidate before it is compiled in. Retraining is the commands in the model's provenance and in the notes folder's `s29c-handover.md`.

**How it was checked,** each heavy job under the Mac's lock: FRUSLanguageTests, 48 tests in 6 suites, with the server's `LanguageCommandTests` and the parity target's `LanguageReportTests`, `GoldenTests` building the new golden file's scratch copy; the whole package with `scripts/swift --postgres test`, every test passing with the one named skip (a first run had failed `GoldenTests`, which listed the new file as pending, and a race in S27b's `QueryEncoderTests.itComesBackAfterItIsKilled`, which passed in the second); the image built as `frus-light:s29c`, whose binary prints the committed digest; and `scripts/compose-smoke --e2e` on port 18290 against it, passing, its new step on aarch64.

**Found, not fixed here:** NaturalLanguage tags a demonym before a capital as an adjective where the treebank's tags make it a proper noun, and adverbs and adjectives such as `more` otherwise than the treebank; a class rule would follow it further at the treebank's expense. `No.` and `p.` before a number are left as the rules have them. ## Session 27b: the encoder

23 November 2026 · branch `claude/s27b-encoder-80d939` · [#166](https://github.com/joshbotts/FRUS-Explorer-Web-App/pull/166) · upstream `4556c4d5`, unchanged

Phase 4's row S27b, in wave 1 beside S26a and S29a upstream: search by meaning's encoder and its model, in the image, by the owner's answers of 23 November. No upstream pull request, no pin move and no migration. The branch was cut from #165's head, `b3d6f81`, which merged into `main` as `08b2a1c` meanwhile, and kept in local commits until the push.

**The image** (`docker/Dockerfile`, `NOTICE`):
- **The encoder stage** builds llama.cpp's CPU `llama-server` from source at `a0e6dc7384edb8f5d927155e1d26c10b4a310e6d`, the `LLAMA_COMMIT` of the pinned app's `Scripts/build-llama-xcframework.sh`, fetched at depth 1 and checked, on the runtime's own Ubuntu 24.04 with CMake, Ninja and GCC 13, `GGML_NATIVE=OFF`, on each architecture's own runner. Its options leave out the web UI, which llama.cpp's build otherwise fetches from a Hugging Face bucket as it builds (`LLAMA_USE_PREBUILT_UI=OFF`); HTTPS, which the encoder on 127.0.0.1 does not speak (`LLAMA_OPENSSL=OFF`); and starting processes of its own, which its tools and router mode would (`LLAMA_SUBPROCESS=OFF`). On the owner's Mac, arm64, the stage took 87 s, 50 of them compiling; the binary is 11,347,272 bytes stripped and links `libgomp`, `libstdc++`, `libm`, `libgcc_s` and `libc`, so the runtime gains `libgomp1`. It prints `version: 0.6.0-dev (build 1, commit a0e6dc7)`, the form the app's fixture script reads. Its licence and those of the libraries llama.cpp carries (cpp-httplib, nlohmann/json, xxHash, rotate-bits and a public-domain SHA-256) go to `/usr/share/doc/frus-light/llama.cpp`.
- **The model stage** takes `embeddinggemma-2-Q8_0.gguf` from the folder a build gives as its `model-source` context, or else fetches it from the release the app's `SemanticModelFetcher` names, through the one redirect GitHub answers a release's file with (`curl --max-redirs 1`, https alone; 52 s here), and refuses any file but one of 309,855,456 bytes at SHA-256 `2188ac1d…09135`. Its folder and file have fixed modes and times (15 October 2026, the model's release), and the runtime copies them with `COPY --link`, a layer made apart from the layers below it. Measured: the model's layer is `sha256:33271e45…` in the image, again after the model stage was rebuilt from nothing, the file downloaded anew, and under amd64's Ubuntu as under arm64's, so an install pulls it once a model, on either architecture.
- **The runtime** holds the binary at `/usr/local/bin/llama-server`, the model at `/usr/share/frus-light/model/`, and `NOTICE` beside `LICENSE`, new: the model, its file, size, digest and licence, Apache 2.0, and llama.cpp's MIT notice, as the app's own `NOTICE` gives them.
- **Its size, on arm64:** `edge` before this row, `sha-16ebe5d`, is 326 MB unpacked and 122 MB to pull (Docker Desktop's "disk usage", 449 MB, adds the two); this row's image is 648 MB unpacked and 410 MB to pull. The model's layer is 310 MB, llama-server's 11.4 MB, and `libgomp1` 0.4 MB.

**CI** (`.github/workflows/ci.yml`, `image.yml`, `scripts/fetch-model`): the compose job and `image.yml`'s builds take the model from the Actions cache by the digest the Dockerfile names, `search-model-<sha256>`, which `scripts/fetch-model` fills once a model with the model stage's own checks, and give it to the build as its `model-source` context, so that no CI build fetches it. On `main`, `image.yml`'s build job also builds frus-parity's image into the build cache, and verify, which now checks out the submodule, loads it from there and passes it to the smoke test, so that checks 2 and 8 and check 9's encoder half run on both architectures; verify's limit is 40 minutes where it was 20. `NOTICE` and `scripts/fetch-model` join `image.yml`'s paths.

**The server** (`Sources/FRUSLightCore/QueryEncoder.swift`, `Configuration.swift`, `Sources/FRUSLightAPI/AdminSemantic.swift`, `Application.swift`):
- `Package.swift` gives `FRUSLightCore` and `FRUSLightAPI` SemanticVectorsKit: the kit's `SemanticQueryPrompt.queryPrefix`, and its `SemanticVectorsArtifacts.Index`, through which the server reads `provenance.modelFileSHA256` from the bundled `semantic-vectors-index.json`.
- `FRUS_ENCODER`, `on` by default; `off` keeps the encoder from starting, and the server says so in its log. The binary's and the model's paths are the image's, with no variable; a test names a stand-in.
- `QueryEncoder`, an actor, the server's one encoder. At its first use it reads the model's SHA-256 once, off the cooperative pool, and holds it to the bundled index's, refusing a model of another digest. At the first query it starts `llama-server` with `Process` on a free port of 127.0.0.1, with a key of that start's own in its environment (`LLAMA_API_KEY`) and nothing of the server's environment but the paths, the locale and `MALLOC_ARENA_MAX`, so that no setting of the server's, a password among them, reaches it; then waits for `/health`. Its command line is the app's load: the model's own context, a physical batch of 2,048, one sequence, pooling and attention as the GGUF declares them and no warm-up, with none of the server's web UI, slots' list or automatic fitting. A query asks `/tokenize` for the prompt's tokens, the model's special tokens included as the embedding counts them, and refuses one past the app's 2,048 in the app's words, "This search is too long for the model. Try a shorter phrasing.", with the count; then `/embedding` with `embd_normalize` −1, the pooled vector as the model computed it, which the server normalises as the app's `SemanticQueryEncoder` does: the sum of squares in double precision, and each value times its inverse square root. Queries at once share one start. The child stops after the app's 180 idle seconds and with the server, through `EncoderService`; a query that finds it gone starts it again, once; its output is kept by line, its last 60, and logged when it fails or ends unasked.
- **Administration ▸ Semantic**, a pane of the library's group: `GET /api/v1/admin/semantic`, Search Model's report, and `GET /api/v1/admin/semantic/embedding?query=`, one query embedded through the server's own path, with its prompt, tokens, vector and time, refused as `QUERY_MISSING` (400), `QUERY_TOO_LONG` (422), `ENCODER_OFF` (409), `ENCODER_UNAVAILABLE` or `ENCODER_FAILED` (503).
- **`frus-light semantic`**, beside `backup` and `user`: the report for a server whose Administration is refused, the encoder's state read from the process table, loaded once its health answers, since the command is not the server and holds no child.

**The browser app** (`web/src/admin/SemanticPane.tsx`, `api/admin.ts`, `copy.ts`, the router and the panes): Search Model, the app's Settings section (`SemanticModelSection`) in a server's words, "In the image and verified — 310 MB on this server.", with the model file, its size, its SHA-256 held to the bundled index's, its licence, the engine at its commit, the encoder off, idle, starting or loaded, with the memory it holds and when it stops, and the app's footer with the model in the image; nothing to download or remove. Read again every ten seconds while the encoder is loaded.

**The parity harness:** `frus-parity embed --api <url>`, check 9's encoder half (`Tests/FRUSParity/EmbedCheck.swift`): each of the 25 queries of the app's `query-parity-fixture-embeddinggemma-2.json` embedded through the route and held to its vector at a cosine of 0.999 or more, the app's bar, refused before any query when the fixture's prompt or model digest is not the server's; with each cosine, as information, how many signs of the first 512 values differ, the bits the Hamming stage reads.

**Tests:** the stand-in, `Tests/EncoderStandIn`, an executable the swift job builds, answers as `llama-server` does: it takes the server's command line and refuses an argument it does not know, listens on 127.0.0.1 alone, will not start without a key and refuses every request but the health check without it, answers 503 while it "loads", and gives `/tokenize` and `/embedding` in llama-server's shapes with vectors of its own, its "model" a file of settings a test writes. `QueryEncoderTests` (14): the child starts at the first query and answers as the app's encoder, a vector equal to the app's normalisation of the stand-in's; queries at once share one start; it stops when idle and starts again; it comes back after a SIGKILL, saying so; off starts none; 2,048 tokens pass and 2,049 are refused in the app's words, and a query past 64 KB without asking; a model not the bundled index's, or no binary, is refused; a failed start says why, with the child's last words; the child's environment and command line; the version line; the normalisation; and the process table. `EncoderImageTests` (6): the Dockerfile's commit is the app script's, and its model the app's file, length and address at the bundled digest; the NOTICE names it; the limit, the prompt and the idle window are the app's; and the app's fixture is of this engine and model. `SemanticRouteTests` (5), `SemanticCommandTests` (2), `EmbedCheckTests` (4, against a live server over the stand-in, whose end stops the child), `SemanticMirrorParityTests` (2: the refusals' words and Search Model's, held to the app's source) and `Semantic.test.tsx` (4); `AdminRouteTests` lists the two routes. Playwright's `admin-semantic.spec.ts` embeds a query through the server's path, reaches Search Model by keyboard from Status, reads it with the real encoder loaded, and checks axe.

**The runs,** on the owner's Mac under the heavy lock, which the two upstream sessions' Mac checks shared, from `131dc1c` with this entry's tests:
- **Swift:** `scripts/swift --postgres test`, 4,432 tests, all passing; the one skip, `backupExclusion()`.
- **The browser app:** typecheck, lint, 731 unit tests in 81 files, and the build.
- **The image and the smoke test:** the image as `frus-light:s27b` in 307 s on the warm cache mount, frus-parity's in 44, and `FRUS_IMAGE=frus-light:s27b FRUS_PARITY_IMAGE=frus-light:s27b-parity FRUS_HOST_PORT=18270 scripts/compose-smoke --e2e`, passing in 551 s: llama-server at `a0e6dc7` and the model at the bundled digest in the image; the first query embedded through the server's path in the hardened container, read-only, with no capability, as UID 10001, in 0.48 s with the encoder's start and the model's digest; Search Model and `frus-light semantic` finding it loaded on 127.0.0.1 alone; check 9's encoder half passing; and the browser suite, 96 passing with the 9 specs other phases run, at the root and under the path.

**CI.** The first run's swift job failed `itStopsWhenIdleAndStartsAgainAtTheNextQuery`: on a loaded runner, where the test took 34 s, its 400 ms idle window stopped the child before the report the test read its process from. The test now takes each process from the encoder's "started" line, which the start logs before its query returns, and waits for the idle stop's line; its waits allow 30 s, and a failed start waits 3 s for the child's last words. The encoder's suites then passed three times over, and pinned to one CPU. The image's builds passed on both architectures, in 13 minutes each. The compose job's limit is 60 minutes where it was 45: with nothing cached, as after this row's change to `Package.swift`, its image took 12.7 minutes to build, where `main`'s whole job takes 23 with the image cached.

## Phase 4's decisions: the owner's answers

23 November 2026 · branch `claude/phase-4-decisions-f837c3` · [#165](https://github.com/joshbotts/FRUS-Explorer-Web-App/pull/165) · upstream `4556c4d5`, unchanged

The owner started phase 4 by asking for each decision it waited on, with a recommendation, the other feasible options and a choice that told more of each, and answered them here in three rounds. This session changes records only: nothing under `web/`, `Sources/`, `Tests/`, `fixtures/`, `scripts/`, `docker/` or `.github/`. Ten decisions were open: the plan's nine and phase 3's Gotenberg checkpoint, which S30d's packet now leans on.

**The answers** (`PLAN.md`, Answered on 23 November, for phase 4):

- **Three sessions at once,** not four, for the usage limit: in phase 3 three Opus sessions at the highest effort already spent a five-hour window. The waves are drawn again for three, ten where four took eight, with the upstream rows and the pin moves first.
- **The Manually Annotated Sub-Corpus** for the tagger, from the American National Corpus's own site; the owner reads its licence there before S29c commits a model.
- **The model in the image,** where SPEC and S27b's default had an admin download it, the owner's choice over the session's recommendation; and with the model there, **the encoder on by default,** as recommended.
- **Every vector in the image too,** for every server. The owner first chose every volume's vectors fetched at a server's first start, then asked whether they could be in the image and still take volumes published or much corrected later. The session read the app's generator, its shard store and the vectors' host, and found that a re-pack is one set: the bundled tier, its index and the shard manifest change with the shards, and no shard is usable ahead of the bundled files that name it, since the Hamming stage scans the bundled sign bits, a document's identity is the bundled index's alone and each shard is held to the bundled manifest's digest. So updates come at pin moves, and the image keeps the generation's shards in a base layer and a re-pack's in a small layer beside it. The owner chose that, and filed for after phase 4 a server that embeds a new or corrected volume itself with the model in its image.
- **The rest as recommended:** a reader's request fetches nothing, which the vectors' answer settled, since there is nothing to fetch; check 9 in two halves; the golden files made by the row's session on the owner's Mac; the Word Cloud's Compare with…, its exports, a collection's cloud and the map's PDF after phase 4; and Gotenberg acceptable. **Against the recommendation, no web visit in the Mac:** tests suffice, and the checkpoint is dropped.

**Checked on 23 November:**

- **The vectors' host,** `joshbotts/frus-semantic-vectors`: `generations/89481b18/shards-manifest.json` at `9be645e9`, the folder's only commit, is the app's bundled manifest at the pin byte for byte (SHA-256 `a8ed3e80…`), so the image can fetch the shards at that commit. Within a family the host has been updated twice, `dd8295fe` (a volume added, 10 September) and `08e4817b` (two corrected volumes' shards replaced in place, 10 October), and it holds no index, binary or map.
- **MASC's terms:** the ANC distributes it with no restriction on redistribution or use, where LDC's catalogue copies (LDC2010T22, LDC2013T12) carry LDC's user agreement.

## Phase 4's plan: semantic and language, on four tracks

23 November 2026 · branch `claude/vigilant-galileo-eylx4k` · [#164](https://github.com/joshbotts/FRUS-Explorer-Web-App/pull/164) · upstream `4556c4d5`, unchanged

The owner asked for a development plan for phase 4, which the plan had named next "once it is planned" when phase 3 was signed off that morning (Session 25b). This session changes records only: nothing under `web/`, `Sources/`, `Tests/`, `fixtures/`, `scripts/`, `docker/` or `.github/`. It planned the phase in rows of one pull request each, as phases 2 and 3 were, from the app's code at the pin, and it measured the phase's two largest unknowns on Linux before writing a row that rested on them.

**What phase 3 cost,** read on 23 November from the repository's history, since the arrangement it ran under is the one phase 4 keeps:

- **69 pull requests,** between #94 and #163, merged between 7 and 23 November.
- **Nine merges of `main` into an open branch,** where phase 2's forty pull requests had forty-one.
- **The files most changed,** by commits that are not merges: the log 109, SPEC 70, PLAN 69, `copy.ts` 51, INSTALL 38, `app.css` 36, `compose-smoke` 34, the README 25, `Routes.swift` 22, COORDINATION 21, `router.tsx` 15, `UserData.swift` 12, `Package.swift` and the Dockerfile 6 each, `web/package.json` 1.
- **CI's runs were not counted.** The agent sent to count them was stopped by the usage limit, and listing them again would have cost more than the number is worth to this plan; the next session that reads GitHub's records can count them against the arrangement's measure, two runs a pull request.

**Checked against the app's code at the pin** (`docs/prep/README.md`, Phase 4), by six read-only surveys, each claim that sizes a row read again here:

- **The semantic half's arithmetic is the kits' already.** SemanticVectorsKit, 2,309 lines, is public, Foundation-only and tested on Linux in CI: it reads the bundled tier, the shards and the map, quantizes a query and runs both stages of the retrieval. Everything on it is app code: the shard store and the fetcher's rules, the three passes of Related Documents' semantic axis (510 lines over `AppState`) and Project Home's reach, the searcher (519) and the backend (592) of search by meaning, the model's store, and the map's rules, in six small files and a 3,492-line view. FRUSCoreKit depends on neither SemanticVectorsKit nor WordCloudKit, and its boundary test permits neither.
- **Search by meaning.** The app's encoder calls llama.cpp through a vendored framework, pinned at `a0e6dc73` since 15 October, the commit the corpus's vectors were embedded through; SPEC still named `8663224`, which cannot run EmbeddingGemma 2. The model has had no consent step since build 51. The app holds its own encoder to a cosine of 0.999 against the llama.cpp command line over 25 judged queries, whose reference vectors are committed. The "600 corpus-gate queries" of SPEC's check 9 were corpus rows, and their reference lists are not in the app's repository; and the app's own ladder says that a re-embedded query cannot be held to an exact list.
- **Search Within These Results** (the app's #1577, of 18 October) layers Meaning with Keywords, so the web has neither half, and SPEC, written before it, does not name it.
- **The map** is 314,616 points in 140 regions, six bytes a point, row for row the vectors' index; SPEC said 314,571 in three places. Its lenses, picking, lasso, axis and export are pure app code, its renderer Metal's. Browse's clusters read the same files, and the web's Browse has left them out since phase 1.
- **Language.** WordCloudKit counts through `NLTagger` alone and marks every tagging declaration unavailable on Linux. But it already describes a tagger that does less than Apple's, in the three flags of `NaturalLanguageHealth`, and keeps a second reference counted without lemmas, for a launch with no lemmatiser. No file names the tokenizer that counted it, so SPEC's rule that a reference from another tokenizer is never compared is stated by no code. The live count, the keyness ranking, the scopes and the collocates are app code, Foundation-only but for the scopes' resolver.
- **Archives Visits** is 4,110 lines of Foundation-only app code in eight files over the kit's Source Explorer, with a derivation that reads SwiftData rows; its one composition is a text, and its PDF is that text.
- **The server:** it starts no process; its library's transport follows no redirect to another host, which the model's address answers with; the swift job may skip nothing, so a test cannot be gated on the model; the image already ships every semantic file and both references, and reads none; migrations stand at 8; the three visit tables have been there since migration 2, with no route.

**Built, to measure,** on the session's host (Ubuntu 24.04, x86-64, 4 vCPUs), nothing of it committed:

- **llama.cpp at the app's commit** builds `llama-server` and `llama-embedding` in 118 s; `llama-server` is 15.9 MB and links `libgomp`, which the runtime image lacks.
- **The app's 25 queries, embedded on Linux** with the app's own fixture script and the model, whose SHA-256 is the app's: a least cosine of 0.999692 against the app's committed fixture through `llama-embedding`, and 0.999866 through `llama-server`, the same vectors at 1, 2 and 4 threads. The server is ready in 1.2 s, holds 425 MB, and answers a warm query in a median of 38 to 89 ms.
- **Linux's Foundation splits no words:** `byWords` is marked unavailable in `swift:6.4-noble`. A splitter written by hand counted a fixture volume at about eight million words a second.

**The plan** (`PLAN.md`, Phase 4) has 26 rows in six groups, on four tracks, Semantic, Map, Language and Visits, with Upstream and the pin moves apart:

- **S26, the vectors and Related Documents:** the stores and the semantic source upstream (S26a), the first pin move (S26b), the vectors on the server with check 9's kernel half on the fixtures (S26c), and the semantic axis with Beyond your library, the reach and the feedback, migration 9 (S26d).
- **S27, the encoder and search by meaning:** the engine upstream (S27a), the encoder (S27b), the second pin move (S27c), search by meaning (S27d), and Search Within These Results with the fallback (S27e).
- **S28, the map and Browse's clusters:** the rules upstream (S28a), the canvas (S28b), the reading (S28c), Browse's clusters (S28d) and the tools (S28e).
- **S29, language:** the tagger's seam upstream (S29a), the live counts, the ranking and the collocates upstream (S29b), the web's tagger (S29c), the family's clouds and references (S29d), live word clouds (S29e), Distinctive and Collocates (S29f), and the shares chips (S29g).
- **S30, Archives Visits:** the packet upstream (S30a), the derivation over values upstream (S30b), the list and the editor (S30c), and the packet with the ways in (S30d).
- **S31:** the sign-off, check 9 at full scale.

Seven upstream pull requests in two batches, two pin moves, fourteen owner checkpoints, nine risks, thirteen decisions and nine open questions. Phase 3's arrangement stands; what changes is the tracks, and the files each row may touch. Check 9 is read in two halves: a cosine for the encoder, and identical lists for the kernel over the same rows; the agreement of the two encoders' lists is reported.

**What the plan decides that SPEC did not:** the tagger is the web's own code, as the rich-text codec is, behind a seam in the kit; once it has counted the corpus, the web counts in one family and reads the Mac's bundled clouds no more; downloads are an admin's, so a reader's request fetches no vectors, where the app's does; Search Within These Results and Browse's clusters join the phase; and the entity lenses stay phase 5's.

**How the session went.** Six surveys ran at once, and with a dry-run build beside them the session met the owner's usage limit: three agents stopped. When it reset, the map's survey was resumed, the language survey was read by the session itself, and the count of CI's runs was given up. The plan takes the lesson as a risk and a rule: its waves never ask for more than four sessions, and the surveys' findings are kept with file and line so that no row reads the app again.

**Records**

- **`docs/PLAN.md`:** the Phase 4 section, with its flowchart, the rows, check 9's reading, what changes in the arrangement, the waves and a stub for each row's done paragraph; the Summary's line on where the plan stands; the session plan's line on phase 4; nine owner checkpoints, fourteen steps, with the golden-files row and the paragraph on what a Mac check costs; nine risks; and the two answer sections.

No upstream pull request, no pin move, no migration, and nothing under `Sources/` or `web/`: the parity harness alone (`Tests/FRUSParity`, the `frus-parity` command and their tests), and the records.

**The full corpus, on both sides.**
- **The server:** the owner's Standalone install, a Compose project beside their own on port 8081. It downloaded the 553 volumes on 15 November and indexed them again at index version 75 on 22 November, under `:1.0-1861.1` (the indexer at `08e8bac8`, which the pin's `4556c4d5` leaves as it was: the three pull requests past the tag change Related Documents', Chronology's and Corpus Analytics' reads, and nothing the indexer stores). On the owner's word ("Yes, S25b moves it"), this session moved it to `main`'s build, `sha-b138633`, at 03:04Z on 23 November: ready six seconds later, nothing queued or re-indexed, its index the same file (size, modification time and SQLite's change counter), its `.env` kept as `.env.bak-2026-11-23`. Nothing on the three checks' paths changed between the two builds.
- **The Mac's side:** the owner's full export from FRUS Explorer 1.0 (1861), made on 22 November without the writing (index 75, FTS generation 4, 553 volumes, 321,749 documents), opened read-only and immutable, never committed.
- **The same files:** index 75 records the file each volume was indexed from (FRUS-Explorer#1909), and all 553 volumes have the same git blob SHA-1 and size in both indexes. The server's index was copied once, through a read-only mount of its volume, while no job ran.

**Check 2 at full scale: passes.** S12d's pin move found the index summary refusing the owner's full export: its library, which the app has upgraded in place since before index version 69, keeps `cross_references.is_broken` and `external_citations.note_label` last, where an upgrade's `ALTER TABLE … ADD COLUMN` appended them, and `person_mentions` without the `UNIQUE` a later version declares. Of the two ways S12d's entry named, the row took the summary that reads an upgraded library, which needs nothing of the owner's Mac, since the files are the same; the orchestrator agreed.
- **What a library's history holds apart from its index,** measured on the export: the two columns' places; the missing constraint, whose table holds 616,944 mentions, every one distinct; 161 revision rows of documents the corpus dropped since, at index version 62, `vanished`, in 75 volumes; 172 rows of revision history; and the order of a volume's documents (below).
- **`frus-parity summarize --library`** reads the index such a library holds. Every hash already selects its columns by name, so their places change nothing, and a table's columns are checked as a set. The schema is gated by each table's columns, with their types, defaults and keys, and by every index's, trigger's and virtual table's statement, with its layout set aside. The revisions of the documents the index holds are gated, all at version 75. Information, never compared: the tables' stored text, their `UNIQUE` and primary-key constraints, the dropped documents' revisions, the revision history, and `document_cache`'s order. A library summary is never a golden file: `check-golden` refuses one, and `compare-summary` refuses to compare one with a golden summary. A golden summary is byte for byte as before.
- **Two corrections made in the app,** which the export carries and the server's index, which no curator has corrected, does not: `frus1943`'s `ch2subsubch11`, headed "Editorial note", reclassified as an editorial note; and frus1945Berlinv02's "Army General A. I. Antonov", a record whose ref is malformed (", Chief of Staff of the Red Army"), merged with "Antonov, Alexey Innokentyevich" (frus1943CairoTehran `p_AAI1`), so the export holds 18,018 rollups and 167 candidate pairs where the server's index holds 18,019 and 168. Both are the app's overrides of a reader's, which it replays into its index; it bundles none. `frus-parity apply-corrections` gives the same two to a copy of the server's index through the kit's own calls, `applyClassificationOverrides` and `consolidatePersonRollup(overrides:)`, as a Standalone server's curator gives them (`IndexCorrections`), and folds the log into the file.
- **The run,** in the container, on an APFS clone of the export and the copy of the server's index, first from `3ecf4b5`, each library summary in 33 and 38 s, and again from `56bcb7f`, which gates AUTOINCREMENT too, in 43 and 51 s beside checks 7 and 8, with the same result. Before the corrections, six gating differences, every one theirs: `document_cache` in frus1943, `person_rollup`, `person_rollup_member` in frus1945Berlinv02 and `person_cluster_candidate`. With them given to a clone of the copy: **"check 2 passes: 34 digests and 5 checks are identical"**, the integrity checks and the instance-mode vocabularies left out above 64 MB, as for any large file. Information: the dropped revisions (161 and 0), the history (172 and 0), the stored schema (85 statements and 86), its constraints (39 rows and 42), the export's own research tables, the rollups' numbers, the structure JSON's key order, and the order of documents.
- **The order of a volume's documents,** which the app lists by rowid (`documents(forVolume:)`), is a library's history too. The kit writes `document_cache` by upsert (`ON CONFLICT(volume_id, document_id) DO UPDATE`), which keeps a row's rowid when its volume is indexed again, where it deletes and writes again the other tables a volume's pass stores; so a document an index version began to hold, or a corrected file added, comes after the rows its volume already had. `page_ranges`' and `cross_references`' orders, which the app reads too, are identical over the full corpus, and still gate in a library summary. `frus-parity compare-order` reports `document_cache`'s, volume by volume: 192 volumes in the index's order; 357 whose rows fall in runs of consecutive rowids, one to an indexing pass, each run in the index's order (951 runs, 157 of them a single row, which says least, and 35,271 rows after a volume's first run); and 4 out of the index's order within a run, frus1902app1 (`s05sub03` before `s05`), frus1943CairoTehran (`ch12subsubch24` before `ch12subsubch23`), frus1945Berlinv02 (`d710a-83` before `d710a-82`) and frus1945Malta (`ch8subch22` before `ch8subch21`), where an earlier pass stored them so, from an earlier file or indexer, which the export alone cannot say. frus1969-76ve09p1's "notes" section is third in a fresh index, the server's and the owner's golden library's, and last in the owner's full library. The fixtures' order still gates in CI against the golden library, which indexed them in one pass. A full export from a library made in one pass would have gated it at full scale too, at hours of the owner's Mac.

## Session 24i: the Word Cloud

23 November 2026 · branch `claude/inspiring-dijkstra-931fb5` · [#162](https://github.com/joshbotts/FRUS-Explorer-Web-App/pull/162) · upstream `4556c4d5`, unchanged

Phase 3's row S24i, the features track's wave 9 and the S24 group's last row: the Word Cloud in Frequency mode, over WordCloudKit, which S24d's FRUS-Explorer#1900 made build on Linux and S24e's pin move compiled. The branch was cut from `main` at `85aff64`, #159's merge, and kept in local commits until the push. No upstream pull request, no pin move, no migration, no lockfile change; `Package.swift` gives `FRUSLightAPI` and the parity tests WordCloudKit, the line S24d's hand-over left for this row.

**The kit's members, all public.** The survey found every member the row reads public at the pin, so nothing was written around and nothing went to the orchestrator for an issue: `CloudVectorsFile(contentsOf:)` with its provenance, lists and entries; `WordCloudLens` (`bundledCloudLenses`, `isSignalDependent`, `minimumSignalTerms`, `colorsBySentiment`); `WordCloudTuning(settingsMinimumLength:minimumCount:foldPlurals:filterMarkings:)` and `.standard`; `WordCloudTokenizer`'s initialiser and `accepts(_:)`, its filters, which read no tagger and stay on Linux; `WordCloudStopwordSet` and `WordCloudLexiconSet` by URL, `active(includeDiplomatic:)`, `markings`, `filter(for:)` and `polarity(of:)`; `TermCount`; `KeynessCloudMeasure`; `KeynessBaselineFile.Configuration.mismatches(against:…)`; and `CountCopy`. What the app's view decides between them is app code, mirrored and held to its source: `BundledCloudVectors.terms(forScope:lens:)` and `list(in:scope:lens:)`, `LensChip`'s label, `WordCloudTokenizer.configured`, `WordCloudBench.evaluate` and its canonical sample, `WordCloudSettings`' lists and their adds and removals, `SettingsSyncCoordinator`'s JSON, `WordCloudDisplayState.resolve`, its count line and messages, `WordCloudScopeBar`'s menu, the resolver's titles, `scopedAnalyzeMenuLabel` and `analyticsScope()`, `WordCloudLayout`, the palette, the typefaces and densities, `WordCloudSettingsView`'s sections and `SampleTermsRow`.

**The bundled data's path.** The image copies the submodule's `FRUSExplorer/Resources` whole, so `cloud-vectors-core.json`, `cloud-vectors-volumes.json`, `word-cloud-stopwords.json` and `word-cloud-lexicons.json` are in `/usr/share/frus-light/resources`; the tests read the submodule's own. The server decodes each on its first use, off the cooperative pool, by the kit's loader (`BundledClouds`, held by `ServerResources`), the volumes file only for a volume's cloud, as the app decodes it once a volume is chosen. Every list holds fifty words and none is flagged below its lens's signal threshold, so a thin volume's fall-back to its era is held over values.

**The server** (`Sources/FRUSLightAPI/WordCloud.swift`; one line each in `Routes.swift`, `UserData.swift` and `ServerResources.swift` beside their kin; `Preferences.swift`):
- **`GET /api/v1/cloud/context`** gives the four lenses in the app's bar's order and words, the two measures, the scope menu (Entire Corpus, the catalogue's subseries in order, each with its volumes by title) and the bundled clouds' own account, the web's sentence over the file's provenance.
- **`GET /api/v1/cloud?scope=&lens=`** gives a scope's cloud, named by the app's own scope signature (`corpus`, `sub:<id>`, `vol:<id>`): its title as the app's resolver gives it, the chip, the state and its words (`noTerms`, `insufficientSignal`, or the web's `noCloud`), the count line by `CountCopy`'s rule, the words the reader's settings keep with their counts and, on the sentiment lens, the kit's lexicon's polarity, how many the list holds and the settings took out, the settings it cannot show, and the scoped hand-off. A request that acts for a user reads their settings from their synced preferences (`SearchUsers.requestUser`, made internal); one that acts for no one reads the app's own. Refused: a subseries the published catalogue does not name (`INVALID_PARAMETER`, as the analytics routes refuse one), an unknown volume (`VOLUME_NOT_FOUND`), a lens the clouds do not carry, and a live scope (`LIVE_SCOPE`, 422): every other signature of the app's, `doc:` to `daterange:`, read as the app's `WordCloudScope.init?(signature:)` reads it (mirrored), a malformed one being a bad parameter.
- **The reader's settings:** `PATCH /me/preferences` takes `wordCloud`'s five criteria, each within its control's range (2 to 8, 1 to 20), an unknown key refused; `POST /me/preferences/hidden-words` and `DELETE …?word=&lens=` hide and show a word as the app's settings do, inside the store's write of the row as it finds it, writing nothing for a change that alters nothing, the lists stored as the app syncs them; `GET /me/preferences/word-cloud-sample` is the settings bench over the stand-in sample. The preferences answer carries each lens's list decoded (`lensStopwords`).

**The browser app** (`web/src/cloud/CloudScreen.tsx`, `cloudRules.ts` with its test, `CloudScreen.test.tsx`, `web/src/api/cloud.ts`, `web/src/settings/WordCloudSettings.tsx` with its test; lines in `router.tsx`, `AppShell.tsx`, `SettingsPanes.tsx`, `ReaderScreen.tsx`, `copy.ts` and `app.css` beside their kin; Search's `Readings.tsx`): `/cloud`, the header's Analytics menu's item after Chronology, and the rail's Word Cloud tile, after Cite.
